data.content:
God
God is portrayed as the divine Creator of heaven, earth, light, plants, animals, and humanity. God creates man and woman in the divine likeness, blesses them, gives commands, and rests after completing creation. God establishes human accountability for bloodshed and is associated with the angels seen in Jacob’s ladder vision.

God walks with Enoch and takes him, observes human wickedness, and instructs Noah to build an ark for the destruction of corrupt flesh. Identified also as the LORD, God brings the Flood, remembers Noah, sends a wind over the earth, speaks to and blesses Noah and his sons, establishes a covenant, and promises never again to destroy all living things by such a catastrophe. God hears Hagar’s affliction, appears and speaks to Abraham, protects Sarah, enables Isaac’s birth, heals Abimelech’s household, and establishes covenants and promises concerning Abraham’s descendants. God instructs Abraham regarding the offering, is feared and obeyed by him, promises Isaac, blesses Ishmael, investigates the wrongdoing of Sodom and Gomorrah, and destroys the cities of the plain while rescuing Lot for Abraham’s sake.

God blesses Isaac with heavenly dew, earthly abundance, grain, and wine. As the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, God hears prayers, observes affliction, enables conception, opens Rachel’s womb, and graciously gives Jacob children. God protects Jacob from Laban, blesses Laban for Jacob’s sake, alters the cattle’s breeding, appears to Laban in a dream, and serves as witness and judge. God directs Jacob to Bethel to dwell and build an altar, accompanies him with divine terror, answers him in distress, promises land and descendants, and commands his return to his ancestral land and kindred.

God is identified by Joseph as the authority against whom sexual wrongdoing is sin and as the source of dream interpretation. God reveals future events, provides Pharaoh’s answer through Joseph, establishes the prophesied outcomes, and raises Joseph to authority in Egypt to preserve life. Joseph fears and credits God for his circumstances, including forgetfulness and fruitfulness, while his brothers invoke God in recognizing revealed iniquity and questioning their returned money. God appears to Jacob in a nighttime vision as the God of Isaac, promises to accompany him into Egypt, gives Joseph his sons, feeds Jacob throughout his life, blesses his descendants, and remains with his family. Ultimately, God turns intended evil toward good, saves many people, visits Israel’s children, and fulfills the oath made to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

Heaven
Heaven is the created celestial domain identified with the firmament and the upper realm. In the flood narrative, its windows open to release rain, making Heaven the heavenly region associated with the onset of the Deluge.

Heaven is described as belonging to the Most High God and as the setting from which Abram observes the stars. It is also the source from which the LORD sends brimstone and fire upon Sodom and Gomorrah, and from which dew descends in the blessing given to Isaac.

In Jacob’s dream, Heaven is the upper destination reached by the ladder and is associated with the gate revealed in his sacred vision. This connection leads Jacob to name the place Bethel, presenting Heaven both as a divine realm and as the celestial destination linked to the gateway between Heaven and earth.

Earth
Earth is the created terrestrial domain and inhabited world containing dry land, the ground, vegetation, animals, and humanity. It is presented as the realm possessed by the Most High God and as the source of agricultural abundance in Isaac’s blessing.

Earth is also the setting of major human events and divine judgment. Cain was cursed and driven away from it, and it became corrupt and filled with violence because of human wickedness. The terrestrial world was subsequently covered by the waters of the flood; the waters later receded, the earth dried, and it was designated as the place where living creatures would multiply.

After the flood, Earth was replenished and overspread by Noah’s descendants and included within God’s covenant. It is also the world across whose surface the LORD scattered people, emphasizing its role as the inhabited realm of human communities and history.

Darkness
Darkness covers the deep and is separated from light by God.

Deep
The deep is the primordial watery expanse over which darkness lies.

Spirit Of God
The Spirit of God moves upon the face of the waters during creation.

Waters
The waters cover the primordial earth and are divided by the firmament.<SEP>The waters prevailed over the earth, covered the mountains, gradually abated, and eventually dried from the earth.

Genesis
Genesis is a biblical book containing an account of creation, including the formation of heaven, earth, living creatures, and humanity.

Light
Light is created by God, separated from darkness, and associated with the day.

Day
Day is the name God gives to the light and is distinguished from night.

Night
Night is the name God gives to the darkness and is distinguished from day.

Firmament
The firmament is an expanse made by God to divide the waters and later called Heaven.

Seas
Seas are the gathered waters separated from the dry land.

Grass
Grass is vegetation brought forth by the earth as seed-bearing plant life.

Herb
Herbs are seed-bearing plants provided as food for humanity and living creatures.

Fruit Tree
Fruit trees are plants that produce fruit containing seed.

Stars
Stars are celestial lights made by God and placed in the firmament.<SEP>The stars are celestial objects used by the LORD to illustrate the innumerable future seed of Abram.

Living Creatures
Living creatures include aquatic animals, birds, cattle, creeping things, and beasts of the earth.

Great Whales
Great whales are large aquatic creatures created by God.

Fowl
Fowl are winged creatures created to fly above the earth and multiply.<SEP>Fowl were among the living creatures destroyed by the waters and were later brought out of the ark and included in Noah's offerings.

Beast Of The Earth
Beasts of the earth are land animals created according to their kinds.

Creeping Thing
Creeping things are terrestrial creatures that move upon the earth.<SEP>Creeping things were among the living creatures that the LORD said would be destroyed from the face of the earth.

Man
Man represents male and female humanity created in the image and likeness of God.<SEP>Man refers to humanity, which multiplied on the earth, became wicked, and was subject to divine judgment.<SEP>Humanity, whose blood is subject to divine accountability and whose creation is described as being in God's image.<SEP>Man was among the living beings who died during the flood and was referenced in God's promise concerning the ground.

Fish
Fish are aquatic creatures placed under human dominion.<SEP>Fish of the sea were described as being delivered into the hand of Noah and his sons.

Evening
Evening is the period paired with morning to mark the successive days of creation.

Morning
Morning is the period paired with evening to mark the successive days of creation.

First Day
The first day is the creation period during which God creates light and separates it from darkness.

Second Day
The second day is the creation period during which God creates and names the firmament.

Third Day
The third day is the creation period during which God gathers the waters, reveals dry land, and brings forth vegetation.

Fourth Day
The fourth day is the creation period during which God makes lights for the firmament to govern day and night.

Fifth Day
The fifth day is the creation period during which God creates aquatic creatures and winged fowl.

Signs
Signs are purposes assigned to the lights in the firmament.

Seasons
Seasons are periods that the lights in the firmament are assigned to mark.

Years
Years are time periods that the lights in the firmament are assigned to mark.

Greater Light
The greater light is a celestial light made to rule the day.

Lesser Light
The lesser light is a celestial light made to rule the night.

Fruit
The fruit came from the trees of the garden, including the tree in the midst of the garden, and was eaten by Eve and Adam.<SEP>Fruit is produced by fruit trees and contains seed.

Adam
Adam is the man formed by God from the dust of the ground, placed in the Garden of Eden, and given authority to name living creatures.<SEP>Adam is Eve's husband who ate the forbidden fruit, hid in the garden, received judgment from the LORD God, and became the father of Cain and Abel.<SEP>Adam is the first human described in the generations, created in God's likeness, and the father of Seth.

Woman
The Woman is formed from Adam’s rib and brought to Adam as a companion and wife.

Serpent
The Serpent is described as more subtle than the beasts of the field and questions the Woman about God’s command.<SEP>The serpent beguiled Eve, denied that eating the forbidden fruit would cause death, and was cursed by the LORD God.

Garden of Eden
The Garden of Eden is a garden planted by God eastward in Eden, containing trees, including the Tree of Life and the Tree of Knowledge of Good and Evil.<SEP>The Garden of Eden is the garden where the tree in the midst of the garden and the tree of life stood, where Adam and Eve hid, and from which Adam was sent away.

Eden
Eden is the region where God plants the garden and from which a river flows to water the garden.<SEP>Eden is the location used to orient the land of Nod, which lies east of Eden.

Tree of Life
The Tree of Life stands in the midst of the Garden of Eden.<SEP>The tree of life was a tree whose fruit could enable continued life, and the way to it was guarded after Adam's expulsion.

data.entity_name: Tree of Knowledge of Good and Evil
data.content:
Tree of Knowledge of Good and Evil
The Tree of Knowledge of Good and Evil stands in the Garden of Eden, and God forbids Adam to eat its fruit.

Pison
Pison is the first river flowing from Eden and encircles the land of Havilah.

Havilah
Havilah is the land encircled by the river Pison and is described as containing gold, bdellium, and onyx stone.<SEP>A son of Cush.<SEP>Havilah is identified as a son of Cush and as a son of Joktan.<SEP>Havilah is the western limit of the region where Ishmael's descendants dwelt.

Gihon
Gihon is the second river flowing from Eden and encircles the land of Ethiopia.

Ethiopia
Ethiopia is the land encircled by the river Gihon.

Hiddekel
Hiddekel is the third river flowing from Eden and runs toward the east of Assyria.

Assyria
Assyria is the region toward which the river Hiddekel runs eastward.<SEP>Assyria is the direction toward which the region of Ishmael's descendants extended from Shur.

Euphrates
Euphrates is the fourth river associated with the river flowing from Eden.<SEP>The Euphrates is the great river marking the eastern boundary of the land promised by the LORD to Abram’s seed.

Heavens
The heavens are part of the created heavens and earth finished by God.

Gold
Gold is a valuable substance found in the land of Havilah and described as good.<SEP>A form of wealth in which Abram is described as being very rich.<SEP>A valuable material included among Abraham's possessions and used for Rebekah's earring and bracelets.

Bdellium
Bdellium is a substance found in the land of Havilah.

Onyx Stone
Onyx stone is a stone found in the land of Havilah.

Sixth Day
The sixth day marks the completion of the creation described before the heavens and earth are finished.

Seventh Day
The seventh day is the day on which God ends the work of creation, rests, blesses the day, and sanctifies it.

Beasts of the Earth
Beasts of the earth are living creatures created by God and given green herbs for food.<SEP>Land animals placed under human authority and included among the living creatures covered by God's covenant.

Fowl of the Air
Fowl of the air are living creatures created by God and given green herbs for food.<SEP>Birds placed under human authority and included among the living creatures covered by God's covenant.

Green Herb
Green herbs are given by God as food for beasts, fowl, and other living creatures.<SEP>The green herb was identified as food comparable to the provision of every living moving thing.<SEP>Vegetation given to humanity as food.

Plants of the Field
Plants of the field are described before they grow in the earth.

Ground
The ground was cursed because of Adam, produced thorns and thistles, and was the source to which Adam would return.<SEP>The ground is watered by mist and provides the dust from which God forms Adam.<SEP>The ground receives Abel's blood and no longer yields its strength to Cain.<SEP>The ground was covered by waters, later became dry, and was mentioned in relation to God's promise not to curse it again.

Dust
Dust from the ground is the material from which God forms Adam.<SEP>Dust was the material from which Adam was taken and to which Adam would return, and it was also assigned as the serpent's food.

Breath of Life
The breath of life is breathed by God into Adam’s nostrils, causing Adam to become a living soul.<SEP>The life-giving breath present in living creatures and used to describe those destroyed outside the ark.

Living Soul
A living soul describes Adam after God breathes the breath of life into Adam.

Rib
A rib taken from Adam is used by God to form the Woman.

River
A river flows from Eden to water the garden and divides into four heads.<SEP>The river beside which Pharaoh stood in his dream, from which the cattle emerged.<SEP>The river is the setting beside which Pharaoh sees the cattle in his dream.

Eve
Eve is Adam's wife and the woman who ate fruit from the tree in the midst of the garden, gave fruit to Adam, and was identified as the mother of all living.

LORD God
The LORD God commanded Adam and Eve not to eat from the tree in the midst of the garden, questioned them after the eating, judged the serpent, Eve, and Adam, clothed Adam and Eve, and sent Adam out of Eden.

data.entity_name: Tree in the Midst of the Garden
data.content:
Tree in the Midst of the Garden
The tree in the midst of the garden was the tree from which the LORD God prohibited Adam and Eve from eating.

Fig Leaves
Fig leaves were sewn together by Adam and Eve to make coverings after their eyes were opened.

Aprons
Aprons were coverings made by Adam and Eve from sewn fig leaves.

Coats of Skins
Coats of skins were made by the LORD God and given to Adam and Eve as clothing.

Cherubims
Cherubims were placed at the east of the Garden of Eden to keep the way to the tree of life.

Flaming Sword
The flaming sword turned in every direction and was placed to keep the way to the tree of life.

Cain
Cain was Adam and Eve's son, a tiller of the ground who brought an offering from the ground and became angry when the LORD God rejected the offering.<SEP>Cain is Adam's son who presents an offering, kills Abel, receives a curse and protective mark from the LORD, leaves the LORD's presence, dwells in Nod, and fathers Enoch.

Abel
Abel was Adam and Eve's son and a keeper of sheep who brought the firstlings and fat of his flock as an offering to the LORD God.<SEP>Abel is Cain's brother whom Cain kills in the field.

Sheep
Sheep were tended by Abel, who kept a flock and brought its firstlings and fat as an offering.<SEP>Livestock given to Abram as part of Pharaoh's favorable treatment of him because of Sarai.<SEP>Sheep belonged to the flocks gathered at the well and were watered and tended by Rachel and Jacob.

Offering
An offering was brought to the LORD God by Cain from the fruit of the ground and by Abel from the firstlings and fat of his flock.<SEP>The offering is presented by Cain but receives no respect from the LORD.

Sin
Sin is described as lying at the door when a person does not do well.<SEP>Sin is described as lying at the door and connected with whether Cain does well.

Trees of the Garden
The trees of the garden produced fruit that the woman said Adam and Eve could eat.

Beasts of the Field
Beasts of the field were included among the animals above which the serpent was cursed.

Seed
Seed represents the descendants of the serpent and the woman in the stated enmity between them.<SEP>Abram's descendants, whom the LORD promises will inherit the land and become as numerous as the dust of the earth.<SEP>The descendants of Abram to whom the LORD promised the land of Canaan.<SEP>The descendants promised to Abram, who were to become as numerous as the dust of the earth and continue forever.<SEP>Seed was provided by Joseph so the people could sow the land after selling their fields to Pharaoh.

Thorns and Thistles
Thorns and thistles were said to grow from the cursed ground for Adam.

Herb of the Field
The herb of the field was food that Adam would eat after the ground was cursed.

Bread
Bread was food that Adam would eat through the sweat of his face.<SEP>Food that Abraham gives to Hagar when sending Hagar and Hagar's son away.<SEP>Bread is food prepared by Rebekah and given to Jacob to present to Isaac.<SEP>Bread was identified by Jacob as food that God might provide during Jacob's journey.<SEP>The food requested by the Egyptians and available in Egypt during the famine.<SEP>Bread is the food Joseph distributed to households and exchanged for money, horses, flocks, cattle, and asses.

Children
Children were to be brought forth by the woman in sorrow.<SEP>Laban's children were claimed by Laban during the dispute and were included in the covenant context.

Good and Evil
Good and evil are forms of knowledge associated with the opened eyes of Adam and Eve and the condition of becoming like gods.

Gods
Gods are beings whom the serpent claimed Adam and Eve would resemble after eating the fruit.

Sorrow
Sorrow was assigned to the woman in conception and childbirth and to Adam in labor for food.

Punishment
Cain describes Cain's punishment as greater than Cain can bear.

Vengeance
Vengeance is prescribed sevenfold against anyone who kills Cain.

Mark Upon Cain
The mark is placed upon Cain by the LORD to prevent anyone who finds Cain from killing Cain.

Land of Nod
The land of Nod is the eastern land where Cain dwells after leaving the LORD's presence.

Cain's Wife
Cain's unnamed wife conceives and bears Enoch.

Enoch
Enoch is Cain's son, the namesake of a city, and the father of Irad.<SEP>Enoch lived sixty-five years before begetting Methuselah, walked with God, and was taken by God at three hundred and sixty-five years.

City of Enoch
The city is built by Cain and named after Cain's son Enoch.

Irad
Irad is Enoch's son and the father of Mehujael.

Mehujael
Mehujael is Irad's son and the father of Methusael.

Methusael
Methusael is Mehujael's son and the father of Lamech.

Lamech
Lamech has two wives, Adah and Zillah, fathers several children, and claims to have slain a man and a young man.<SEP>Lamech lived one hundred and eighty-two years before begetting Noah, named Noah, lived five hundred and ninety-five additional years, and died at seven hundred and seventy-seven years.

Adah
Adah is Lamech's wife and the mother of Jabal and Jubal.<SEP>A daughter of Elon the Hittite and a wife of Esau who bore Eliphaz.<SEP>Adah is Esau's wife and the mother of Eliphaz.

Zillah
Zillah is Lamech's wife and the mother of Tubalcain and Naamah.

Jabal
Jabal is Adah's son and is described as the father of people who dwell in tents and keep cattle.

Jubal
Jubal is Adah's son and is described as the father of musicians who handle the harp and organ.

Tubalcain
Tubalcain is Zillah's son and an instructor of every artificer in brass and iron.

Naamah
Naamah is Zillah's daughter and Tubalcain's sister.

Adam's Wife
Adam's unnamed wife bears Seth again and identifies Seth as another seed appointed in place of Abel.

Seth
Seth is Adam's son, appointed as another seed in place of Abel, and the father of Enos.<SEP>Seth lived nine hundred and twelve years before dying.

Enos
Enos is Seth's son and the father of Cainan.<SEP>Enos lived ninety years before begetting Cainan, lived eight hundred and fifteen additional years, and died at nine hundred and five years.

Cainan
Cainan is Enos's son, born after Enos lives seventy years.<SEP>Cainan lived seventy years before begetting Mahalaleel, lived eight hundred and forty additional years, and died at nine hundred and ten years.

Field
The field is the place where Cain rises against Abel and kills Abel.<SEP>An outdoor area to which Esau went to hunt venison.<SEP>The field is the parcel of land where Jacob spreads his tent and which Jacob purchases from the children of Hamor.

Tents
Tents are dwellings associated with the people for whom Jabal is described as the father.

Harp
The harp is a musical instrument associated with the people for whom Jubal is described as the father.

Organ
The organ is a musical instrument associated with the people for whom Jubal is described as the father.

Brass
Brass is a material used by artificers whom Tubalcain instructs.

Iron
Iron is a material used by artificers whom Tubalcain instructs.

Mahalaleel
Mahalaleel lived sixty-five years before begetting Jared, lived eight hundred and thirty additional years, and died at eight hundred and ninety-five years.

Jared
Jared lived one hundred and sixty-two years before begetting Enoch, lived eight hundred additional years, and died at nine hundred and sixty-two years.

Methuselah
Methuselah lived one hundred and eighty-seven years before begetting Lamech, lived seven hundred and eighty-two additional years, and died at nine hundred and sixty-nine years.

Noah
Noah was described as just and perfect in his generations, walked with God, found grace with the LORD, and begat Shem, Ham, and Japheth.<SEP>A righteous man commanded by God to build the ark, gather provisions and living creatures, and enter the ark with his household.<SEP>Noah remained alive in the ark, released a raven and a dove, removed the ark covering, left the ark with his family, and built an altar to God.<SEP>A man who receives God's covenant, fathers Shem, Ham, and Japheth, plants a vineyard, drinks wine, and lives after the flood for three hundred and fifty years.<SEP>Noah is identified as the ancestor of the families and nations described after the flood.

Shem
Shem was one of the three sons begotten by Noah.<SEP>A son of Noah who enters the ark with Noah, Noah's wife, and the wives of Noah's sons.<SEP>A son of Noah who helps cover Noah's nakedness and whose tents receive Japheth.<SEP>Shem is identified as a son of Noah, the father of Eber, and the ancestor of Elam, Asshur, Arphaxad, Lud, and Aram.<SEP>A patriarch who begat Arphaxad and later had additional sons and daughters.

Ham
Ham was one of the three sons begotten by Noah.<SEP>A son of Noah who enters the ark with Noah, Noah's wife, and the wives of Noah's sons.<SEP>A son of Noah, the father of Canaan, who sees Noah's nakedness and tells his brothers.<SEP>Ham is identified as the father of Cush, Mizraim, Phut, and Canaan, and as an ancestor of nations and families.<SEP>A place where Chedorlaomer's forces defeated the Zuzims.

Japheth
Japheth was one of the three sons begotten by Noah.<SEP>A son of Noah who enters the ark with Noah, Noah's wife, and the wives of Noah's sons.<SEP>A son of Noah who helps cover Noah's nakedness and is described as dwelling in Shem's tents.<SEP>Japheth is identified as the elder brother of Shem.

Sons Of God
The sons of God saw the daughters of men, took chosen women as wives, and fathered children who became mighty men of renown.

Daughters Of Men
The daughters of men were regarded as fair and were taken as wives by the sons of God.

Giants
Giants were present on the earth during the stated period and afterward.

Ark
The ark was an instructed vessel to be made from gopher wood, divided into rooms, and covered inside and outside with pitch; its stated dimensions were three hundred cubits long, fifty cubits wide, and thirty cubits high.<SEP>A large vessel commanded by God and built by Noah from gopher wood, with rooms, a window, a side door, and three stories.<SEP>The ark carried Noah, his family, and living creatures; the ark rested on the mountains of Ararat and was later opened and left.<SEP>The vessel from which Noah's sons and living creatures go forth after the flood.

Beast
Beasts were among the living creatures that the LORD said would be destroyed from the face of the earth.

Fowls Of The Air
Fowls of the air were among the living creatures that the LORD said would be destroyed from the face of the earth.

Flesh
Flesh describes living beings whose ways had become corrupt upon the earth and whom God said would be destroyed.

Gopher Wood
The wood specified by God as the construction material for the ark.<SEP>Gopher wood was the material from which God instructed Noah to make the ark.

Pitch
A substance used to coat the inside and outside of the ark.<SEP>Pitch was the substance used to cover the ark inside and outside.

Noah's Wife
The wife of Noah who enters the ark with Noah and Noah's sons.

Wives of Noah's Sons
The three wives of Noah's sons who enter the ark with Noah's household.

Flood
A catastrophic inundation brought by God that covers the earth, lifts the ark, and causes living creatures outside the ark to die.<SEP>A destructive flood whose waters are stated not to destroy all flesh again under the covenant.<SEP>The flood occurring before Shem begat Arphaxad.

Rain
Rain caused by God to fall upon the earth for forty days and forty nights.<SEP>The rain from heaven was restrained as the floodwaters began to abate.

Great Deep
The great deep whose fountains break up during the onset of the flood.

Food
Edible provisions gathered by Noah for himself and the living creatures in the ark.<SEP>Food is the commodity that Israel's sons travel to Egypt to purchase.

Clean Beasts
Animals classified as clean, taken into the ark by sevens, consisting of male and female pairs.

Unclean Beasts
Animals classified as not clean, taken into the ark by pairs consisting of a male and a female.

Fowls
Birds taken into the ark by sevens or pairs, with male and female representatives.

Creeping Things
Creeping animals of the earth taken into the ark as representatives of their kinds.<SEP>Creeping things were among the living creatures destroyed by the waters and were later brought out of the ark.

Mountains
Elevated landforms covered by the rising floodwaters.

Ark Dimensions
The specified dimensions of the ark: three hundred cubits in length, fifty cubits in breadth, and thirty cubits in height.

Ark Rooms
Compartments commanded for construction inside the ark.

Ark Window
An opening constructed in the ark and finished above.

Ark Door
An entrance set in the side of the ark.

Ark Stories
The lower, second, and third levels specified for the ark.

Living Things
Living creatures brought into the ark in male and female pairs or according to their kinds.<SEP>Living things, including humans and animals, were destroyed by the flood and later brought out of the ark to multiply.

Fountains of the Great Deep
Sources of water that break open at the beginning of the flood.

High Hills
Elevated landforms covered by the floodwaters.

Dry Land
Terrestrial ground on which living creatures exist and from which the flood destroys them.

Seven Days
A seven-day period preceding the arrival of the floodwaters and the onset of rainfall.

Forty Days and Forty Nights
The stated duration of rainfall and the period during which the flood remains upon the earth.

Noah's Age
Noah's stated age of six hundred years when the floodwaters come upon the earth.

Mountains Of Ararat
The mountains of Ararat were the location where the ark rested after the waters began to recede.

Raven
The raven was released by Noah and flew back and forth until the waters dried from the earth.

Dove
The dove was released by Noah several times to determine whether the waters had abated; the dove eventually did not return.

Olive Leaf
The olive leaf was carried in the dove's mouth and indicated to Noah that the waters had abated.

Altar
The altar was built by Noah for burnt offerings to God using clean beasts and clean fowl.<SEP>A structure built by Abram at locations where he worships and calls upon the name of the LORD.<SEP>A worship structure built by Abram in the plain of Mamre unto the LORD.<SEP>Altar built by Abraham at the place designated by God for the burnt offering.<SEP>A structure Isaac built at Beersheba for calling upon the name of the LORD.<SEP>An altar is the structure Jacob is commanded to build at Bethel for God.<SEP>A structure Jacob built at Bethel for God.

Beasts
Beasts were among the living creatures destroyed by the waters and were later brought out of the ark.

Noah's Sons
Noah's sons left the ark with Noah and received God's blessing and instructions to multiply and replenish the earth.

Noah's Wife And Sons' Wives
Noah's wife and his sons' wives left the ark with Noah and his sons.

Wind
The wind was made by God to pass over the earth and contribute to the abatement of the waters.

Fountains Of The Deep
The fountains of the deep were stopped as the floodwaters receded.

Windows Of Heaven
The windows of heaven were stopped, ending the rain from heaven.

Window Of The Ark
The window of the ark was opened by Noah after the waters had begun to decrease.

Covering Of The Ark
The covering of the ark was removed by Noah after the waters had dried from the earth.

Breath Of Life
The breath of life was present in living beings that died during the flood.

Seedtime And Harvest
Seedtime and harvest were described as recurring agricultural cycles that would continue while the earth remained.

Summer And Winter
Summer and winter were described as recurring seasonal cycles that would not cease while the earth remained.

Day And Night
Day and night were described as recurring cycles that would continue while the earth remained.

Gomer
A son of Japheth and the father of Ashkenaz, Riphath, and Togarmah.

Magog
A son of Japheth.

Madai
A son of Japheth.

Javan
A son of Japheth and the father of Elishah, Tarshish, Kittim, and Dodanim.

Tubal
A son of Japheth.

Meshech
A son of Japheth.

Tiras
A son of Japheth.

Ashkenaz
A son of Gomer.

Riphath
A son of Gomer.

Togarmah
A son of Gomer.

Elishah
A son of Javan.

Tarshish
A son of Javan.

Kittim
A son of Javan.

Dodanim
A son of Javan.

Cush
A son of Ham and the father of Seba, Havilah, and Sabtah.<SEP>Cush is identified as a son of Ham and the father of Seba, Havilah, Sabtah, Raamah, Sabtechah, and Nimrod.

Mizraim
A son of Ham.<SEP>Mizraim is identified as a son of Ham and the father of Ludim, Anamim, Lehabim, Naphtuhim, Pathrusim, Casluhim, and Caphtorim.

Phut
A son of Ham.<SEP>Phut is identified as a son of Ham.

Seba
A son of Cush.<SEP>Seba is identified as a son of Cush.

Sabtah
A son of Cush.<SEP>Sabtah is identified as a son of Cush.

Bow
A bow placed in the cloud as the token of God's covenant with the earth and living creatures.<SEP>A weapon Isaac instructed Esau to take while hunting.

Vineyard
A cultivated place planted by Noah.

Wine
A drink consumed by Noah, causing Noah to become drunken.<SEP>Wine is used by Lot's daughters to intoxicate Lot before lying with him.<SEP>Wine is brought to Isaac by Jacob, and wine is included among the provisions mentioned in Isaac's blessing.

Cattle
Cattle are domesticated land animals and livestock described as being created according to their kinds. In the biblical account, they are included among the animals over which the serpent was cursed, and among the livestock associated with the people for whom Jabal is identified as the father. Herd animals representing their kinds were taken into Noah’s ark; cattle were therefore among the living creatures preserved through the flood and brought out afterward. They were also included among the domesticated animals covered by God’s covenant.

Cattle formed an important part of the wealth and pastoral life of Abram and Lot, whose herdsmen disputed because their shared land could not support both households’ livestock. They were among the animals that shepherds were instructed to gather and feed. In the account of Jacob and Laban, cattle included speckled, ringstraked, and grisled animals whose breeding contributed to Jacob’s increasing possessions. Laban’s cattle were tended by Jacob during six years of service, although Laban claimed them as his own. Jacob also owned cattle for which he made booths at Succoth.

During the famine in Egypt, cattle and other livestock—including herds, horses, flocks, and asses—were exchanged with Joseph in return for bread.

Covenant
Covenant refers to several distinct binding or sworn agreements described in biblical narratives.

The Noahic Covenant was established by God with Noah in connection with Noah’s survival in the ark. It extended to Noah’s descendants, living creatures, and the earth, and constituted a divine promise that another destructive flood would not occur.

A covenant between the LORD and Abram concerned the grant of land to Abram’s descendants. Related patriarchal covenants were described as everlasting agreements established by God with Isaac and Isaac’s descendants, and with Abraham, Abraham’s descendants, and the covenant community.

Covenant also denotes agreements between individuals. Abraham and Abimelech made a sworn agreement concerning mutual kindness and truthful dealings. Abimelech and his companions later proposed an agreement with Isaac that included a mutual pledge not to harm one another. Laban and Jacob established a covenant as a witness between them.

LORD
LORD is portrayed as the divine judge, protector, and ruler of humanity and creation. The LORD received the cry of Abel’s blood, questioned Cain, warned him about sin, cursed him, and marked him for protection from being killed. The LORD judged humanity’s wickedness, intended to destroy humanity and other living creatures, yet showed grace to Noah. Observing the city and tower, the LORD confounded human language and scattered the people across the earth.

The LORD appeared to Abram, commanded him, promised land and descendants to his seed, received his worship, and brought plagues upon Pharaoh and his household. Abram built altars to the LORD and invoked him as the Most High God. The LORD is identified as the Most High, possessor of heaven and earth, speaker to Abram, giver of the land, judge of nations, and maker of a covenant with him. The LORD sent angels to destroy Sodom and Gomorrah, destroyed the cities with brimstone and fire, and showed mercy to Lot. The LORD visited Sarah and fulfilled the promise of Isaac’s birth, and was invoked in the angel’s declaration and in the naming of the mountain associated with divine provision.

The LORD guided Abraham’s servant, prospered his journey, appointed Rebekah for Isaac, and was worshiped and invoked as the God of heaven and earth, who blessed Abraham and sent an angel before the servant. The LORD appeared to Isaac, identified himself as the God of Abraham, instructed Isaac to remain in the land, promised blessings and nations to his descendants, blessed his agricultural work and the field whose fragrance Isaac associated with his son, and answered Isaac’s petition concerning Rebekah as well as Rebekah’s inquiry. Jacob declared that the LORD would be his God after his peaceful return to his father’s house and identified the LORD as the source of salvation. The LORD remained with Joseph, showed him mercy, caused his work to prosper, and blessed the Egyptian household for Joseph’s sake.

The Canaanites were present during the dispute between Abram’s and Lot’s herdsmen. Because Abraham lived among them, he prohibited his servant from taking a wife for Isaac from the Canaanite population, indicating a clear distinction between Abraham’s family and the people of the land.

Later, Jacob feared that the Canaanites and other inhabitants of the region would gather against him after the attack on Shechem. The Canaanites also witnessed the mourning at the threshing floor of Atad, recognizing it as an exceptionally grievous mourning conducted by the Egyptians.

Canaan
Canaan refers both to a biblical person and to the land associated with his descendants. Canaan, the son of Ham, was cursed to become a “servant of servants” to his brethren. He was identified as the father of Sidon, Heth, and several Canaanite peoples.

Canaan also denotes the land to which Abram traveled with Sarai and Lot, and which the LORD promised to Abram’s seed and to Abraham’s descendants as an everlasting possession. Abram lived there after separating from Lot. The land included Kirjatharba, identified as Hebron, the city of Shechem, and the field and Cave of Machpelah, including the burial place of Joseph’s father. It was also the land where Rachel died.

In the accounts of Isaac’s and Jacob’s families, Canaan was the region whose daughters Isaac forbade Jacob and Esau to marry. Jacob, Isaac, Esau, and Esau’s family lived in or traveled through it; Esau’s sons were born there and Esau acquired his possessions there. Jacob dwelt in Canaan and intended to return there to his father Isaac.

During the famine, Canaan was the family’s former homeland and a land severely affected by scarcity. Jacob and his sons lived there, and Joseph’s brothers returned there with money and repeatedly traveled from it to obtain grain. Pharaoh instructed them to return to Canaan and bring Jacob and their households to Egypt, from which Jacob and his family ultimately departed. Canaan therefore represents both the ancestral homeland and the divinely promised inheritance of Abraham’s descendants.

Egypt
Egypt is the country to which Abram travels because of a severe famine in Canaan. It is the homeland of Hagar, who is repeatedly identified as Egyptian, and the land from which Hagar’s son receives a wife. Egypt also marks the geographic boundary of Ishmael’s dwelling range and is the country that the LORD instructs Isaac not to enter.

Egypt is ruled by Pharaoh and is associated with his household, royal officers, magicians, and wise men, whom Pharaoh summons to interpret his dreams. The Ishmeelites take Joseph to Egypt, where he is sold to Potiphar and where Potiphar’s household is located. Joseph later interprets Pharaoh’s dreams and governs Egypt during the years of plenty and famine. Under Pharaoh’s authority, Joseph stores and sells food, administers famine relief, acquires land for Pharaoh, and supplies the population during the crisis.

During the famine, Joseph’s brothers travel from Canaan to Egypt to buy corn and appear before him. Joseph invites Jacob and his household to settle there, providing supplies and wagons. Egypt becomes the place where Jacob’s family lives for a time, where Joseph resides, and where Ephraim and Manasseh are born before Jacob’s arrival. Joseph’s family remains there during part of the journey to bury Jacob, and Egypt is ultimately where Joseph dies and is placed in a coffin.

Pharaoh
Pharaoh is the title used for the ruler of Egypt in several narratives, likely referring to different Egyptian kings rather than one identifiable individual. In the account of Abram and Sarai, Pharaoh takes Sarai into his household, enriches Abram because of her, and later confronts and sends Abram away after divine intervention.

Another Pharaoh is the ruler served by Potiphar, who is identified as Pharaoh’s officer and captain of the guard. A further Pharaoh becomes angry with two of his officers and orders them confined in prison. The Pharaoh associated with Joseph is the Egyptian king who dreams of cattle and ears of corn, seeks an interpreter, and summons Joseph from the dungeon. After Joseph interprets the dreams, Pharaoh appoints him over Egypt and directs the people to obtain food from him.

This Pharaoh is also invoked by Joseph’s brothers when they swear that they are not spies, and Judah compares Joseph’s authority with that of Pharaoh. He welcomes Joseph’s brothers, commands them to bring their father and households to Egypt, and provides wagons from Egypt to transport Jacob and his family. He questions Jacob’s family, authorizes their settlement in Goshen, and instructs Joseph to place them in Egypt.

During the famine, Pharaoh is the ruler for whom Joseph acquires the land of Egypt, with the population thereafter owing Pharaoh a fifth of their agricultural produce. Near the end of Jacob’s life, Joseph approaches Pharaoh’s household concerning arrangements for Jacob’s burial, and Pharaoh grants Joseph permission to leave Egypt and bury his father.

Sarah
Sarah, formerly called Sarai, is Abraham’s wife and the mother of Isaac. She is described as Abraham’s paternal half-sister and as a woman who bore Isaac in old age after receiving the promise of his birth while inside her tent. She was also portrayed as a “mother of nations.”

As Isaac’s mother, Sarah objected to Hagar’s son being recognized as heir alongside Isaac. Sarah lived for 127 years and died in Kirjatharba, identified with Hebron in Canaan. Abraham buried her body in the cave of Machpelah, where she is described as being buried with him.

Isaac
Isaac is the son promised by God to Abraham and Sarah and born to them in Abraham’s old age. God established an everlasting covenant with Isaac, through whom Abraham’s seed would be called, and included him among the patriarchs who received the divine oath concerning the future land of the children of Israel. He was Abraham’s beloved son by Sarah and accompanied Abraham to the offering place, where he was bound on the altar before God halted the sacrifice.

Abraham instructed his servant to seek Isaac a wife from Abraham’s country and kindred, and Isaac subsequently married Rebekah, whom the servant encountered in the field. Isaac and Rebekah were the parents of Esau and Jacob. Isaac lived in Gerar, prospered there, dug wells, traveled to Beersheba, received a divine appearance, and made a covenant with Abimelech. He later ate venison, tested Jacob’s identity, blessed both Jacob and Esau, and directed Jacob not to marry a daughter of Canaan.

Isaac was Jacob’s father and was identified by Jacob as the father whose God spoke to him; Jacob also swore by Isaac’s fear and regarded Isaac among the fathers who walked before God. Jacob intended to visit him in Canaan. Isaac lived 180 years and was buried by Esau and Jacob in the Cave of Machpelah with Rebekah.

Abraham
Abraham, formerly called Abram, is a biblical patriarch, prophet, and recipient of God’s covenant and oath. God promised him numerous descendants and the land of Canaan, and Abraham is portrayed as walking before God, obeying the LORD, circumcising the males of his household, and receiving visitors at Mamre. He is the husband of Sarah, the father of Isaac and Ishmael, and later the husband of Keturah. He is also identified as an ancestor of Jacob, whose God invokes Abraham as one of Jacob’s forefathers and as the recipient of the land promised to Jacob and his descendants.

Abraham repeatedly intercedes with the LORD for the righteous in Sodom, then witnesses the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah while God remembers him during Lot’s rescue. He resides for a time in Gerar, makes a covenant with Abimelech, and sends away Hagar and Ishmael. In a supreme test of obedience, he travels with Isaac and two young men, builds an altar, binds Isaac, and prepares a burnt offering, but offers a ram in Isaac’s place. His servants dig wells, and the LORD promises to bless and multiply Isaac’s descendants for Abraham’s sake.

Abraham purchases the field and Cave of Machpelah from Ephron the Hittite, buries Sarah there, and is later buried in the same cave. He gives his inheritance to Isaac and commissions his eldest servant to find Isaac a wife from Abraham’s kindred rather than from among the Canaanites. Thus, Abraham is presented as the foundational patriarch through whom the covenant, ancestral lineage, and promises of land and descendants continue to Isaac and Jacob.

Rebekah
Rebekah was the daughter of Bethuel and the sister of Laban. She is introduced as a woman who drew water for Abraham’s servant and his camels, generously providing for them. Recognized as the woman appointed to become Isaac’s wife, she agreed to leave with the servant and married Isaac.

Rebekah was the mother of Esau and Jacob, and she favored and loved Jacob. After overhearing Isaac instruct Esau to obtain food so that Isaac could bless him, Rebekah directed Jacob to secure the food instead. She prepared savory meat and bread, dressed Jacob in Esau’s clothing, and covered his hands and neck with goat skins so that Isaac would mistake him for Esau and give him the blessing intended for the elder son.

Rebekah later warned Jacob about Esau’s plan against him and sent him to Laban for safety. She was served by Deborah as her nurse and was buried with Isaac in the Cave of Machpelah.

Laban

He became Jacob’s employer and father-in-law, providing his daughters’ handmaids, Bilhah and Zilpah—Bilhah to Rachel and Zilpah to Leah. Laban controlled substantial flocks, negotiated and repeatedly changed Jacob’s wages, and separated livestock belonging to Jacob from his own.

Esau was Isaac and Rebekah’s elder twin and firstborn son, and Jacob’s brother. Described as a cunning or skilled hunter and a man of the field, he prepared savory venison for Isaac. Esau sold his birthright to Jacob in exchange for bread and lentil pottage, and he later reacted bitterly when Jacob received Isaac’s blessing, which Esau had been intended to inherit.

Afterward, Esau hated Jacob and threatened to kill him. When Jacob returned, Esau traveled to meet him with four hundred men. The encounter ended in reconciliation: Esau embraced Jacob, accepted his present, and then returned toward Seir. Esau’s presence is also recalled when God directed Jacob to build an altar at Bethel.

Esau was associated with Edom and is regarded as the father of the Edomites. He eventually moved away from Jacob with his household and was connected with Mount Seir, where he resided. Rachel
Rachel was Laban’s younger daughter, a shepherdess, and Leah’s sister. She became Jacob’s beloved wife after he sought to marry her, and she is associated with Jacob’s household and family. Rachel was also the mistress of Bilhah, whom she gave to Jacob as a secondary wife or concubine.

Initially barren, Rachel conceived after God remembered her and opened her womb, giving birth to Joseph. She was later the mother of Benjamin as well. During Jacob’s approach to Esau, Rachel was among the women to whom Jacob’s children were assigned, and she appears with Joseph during the family’s meeting with Esau.

When Jacob departed from Laban, Rachel stole her father’s household images and concealed them in camel furniture. She remained seated while Laban searched the tent, preventing him from discovering them. Rachel eventually died in Canaan near Ephrath while giving birth to Benjamin and was buried there, near Bethlehem.

Jacob
Jacob, also called Israel, is the younger twin son of Isaac and Rebekah, Esau’s brother, and a plain-dwelling patriarch associated with tents. He acquired Esau’s birthright and, with Rebekah’s preparation—including goat kids—disguised himself as Esau to receive Isaac’s blessing. Fleeing Esau, Jacob traveled to Padanaram, where he dreamed of a ladder reaching heaven and encountered Rachel.

Jacob served Laban for twenty years, working for his daughters and managing Laban’s cattle and flocks. He married Leah, Rachel, Bilhah, and Zilpah, fathering twelve sons and other children, including Dinah. Through negotiated wages and careful management, he gained his own livestock. After God commanded him to return to his ancestral land, Jacob fled with his family and possessions, disputed Laban’s accusations, and made a covenant with him.

Fearing Esau, Jacob prayed, sent him livestock as a gift, crossed the Jordan and Jabbok, and wrestled with an unnamed man, receiving the name Israel. He then met Esau and journeyed with his household through Succoth and Shalem, where he bought land and built an altar. After Dinah’s ordeal involving Hamor and Shechem and the actions of her brothers, God directed Jacob to Bethel, where he erected altars and pillars.

Jacob lived in Canaan, separated from Esau when their possessions became too extensive for them to dwell together, and buried Rachel and Isaac. He was Joseph’s father and mourned him after recognizing his bloodied coat and believing he had been devoured. During famine, Jacob sent his sons to Egypt for food and eventually moved there with his household, including Benjamin. In Egypt he became the grandfather of Ephraim and Manasseh through Joseph, blessed his sons and descendants, assigned inheritances, and requested burial in the cave of Machpelah. He died after gathering his feet into his bed. Jacob is also identified as a recipient of God’s oath concerning the future land of Israel’s descendants.

Leah
Leah was the elder daughter of Laban, Rachel’s sister, and one of Jacob’s wives. Laban gave Leah to Jacob in place of Rachel, whom Jacob intended to marry, making her part of the complicated family history of Jacob’s marriages. Leah later joined Rachel in meeting Jacob in the field and questioned the inheritance available to them from their father’s household.

Leah was the mother of Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, Zebulun, and Dinah. Her children are associated with Jacob’s descendants who later went to Egypt. During Jacob’s approach to Esau, Leah and her children were assigned a designated place within the household arrangement, and Leah was identified among the women and children under Jacob’s protection.

Leah received Zilpah from Laban, and Zilpah is associated with Leah’s household. Leah is also connected with the tent searched by Laban during his pursuit of Jacob’s family. After her death, Leah was buried in the Cave of Machpelah.

Judah
Judah was the fourth son of Jacob and Leah, and the brother of Joseph and Benjamin. He was the father of Er, Onan, Shelah, Pharez, and Zarah. Judah proposed selling Joseph to the Ishmeelites rather than killing him, after which he departed from his brothers, went to Hirah, and married the daughter of Shuah.

Judah was Tamar’s father-in-law through his son Er and the father of Shelah. After failing to give Tamar Shelah as promised, Judah encountered her on the way to Timnath without recognizing her and fathered her twins, Pharez and Zarah. When Tamar’s pregnancy was revealed, Judah acknowledged that she was more righteous than he was.

During the family’s efforts to obtain food from Egypt, Judah reported Joseph’s condition that Benjamin had to accompany the brothers before they could return. He urged Jacob to send Benjamin and pledged responsibility for his safe return. When the brothers later stood before Joseph, Judah spoke on Benjamin’s behalf, pleaded for mercy, and offered himself and his brothers as servants.

Jacob sent Judah ahead of the family to direct Joseph toward Goshen. In Jacob’s blessing, Judah is portrayed as one whom his brothers will praise, victorious over enemies, and symbolized by a lion. He is also associated with enduring rule and the gathering of peoples.

Israel
Israel is the name God gave Jacob after Jacob prevailed in a struggle with a man and with God, replacing his former name. As the ancestral figure Israel, Jacob is the father of the twelve tribes, whose descendants are identified as the sons of Israel.

In the accounts concerning Joseph, Israel is Joseph’s father and loved Joseph more than his other children, giving him a special coat and sending him to find his brothers. He is also identified as the father of Judah, Benjamin, Joseph, and Simeon, and directs his sons to return to Egypt with Benjamin. When Joseph encounters him in Goshen, Jacob is referred to by the name Israel.

Israel appears again in the account of Jacob’s death: Joseph orders the embalming of the body of Israel, the patriarch whose sons became the founders of the twelve tribes. Israel also blesses Joseph’s sons, Ephraim and Manasseh. In addition to referring to Jacob personally, the name Israel denotes the people descended from him who lived and multiplied in Egypt’s land of Goshen.

Joseph
Joseph was the son of Jacob (Israel) and Rachel, whom Rachel named. He was one of Jacob’s younger sons and approached Esau with Rachel. At seventeen, Joseph tended the flock, reported his brothers’ misconduct, received preferential treatment from Jacob, and experienced dreams suggesting that he would exercise authority. His brothers called him a dreamer, cast him into a pit, and sold him to Ishmaelites, who brought him to Egypt.

In Egypt, Joseph was purchased by Potiphar and appointed overseer of his household and possessions. After refusing Potiphar’s wife’s advances, he was falsely accused and imprisoned in a dungeon, where he interpreted the dreams of the chief butler and chief baker. Later summoned by Pharaoh, Joseph interpreted Pharaoh’s dreams as a prophecy of seven plentiful years followed by seven years of famine. Pharaoh appointed him governor and ruler under Pharaoh over Egypt. Joseph stored grain during the abundant years and distributed or sold it during the famine, acquiring land, livestock, and agricultural revenue for Pharaoh while administering Egypt’s resources.

Joseph’s brothers came before him seeking food, though they did not recognize him. He tested their honesty, questioned them, bound Simeon, commanded provisions, restored their money, and arranged a meal while directing his steward and investigating the silver cup. Eventually he revealed himself, forgave them, and brought Jacob and the entire family to Egypt, providing wagons, food, and settlement in the land. He presented the family to Pharaoh, nourished Jacob’s household, and continued caring for them during the famine.

Joseph was the father of Ephraim and Manasseh, whom he presented to Jacob for blessing. Jacob described him as a fruitful bough, protected and blessed by God. Joseph arranged Jacob’s embalming and burial, returned to Egypt, reassured and supported his brothers after Jacob’s death, and died at the age of 110.

Benjamin
Benjamin is Jacob’s youngest son and Rachel’s second child. Rachel named him Benoni before her death, but Jacob renamed him Benjamin. He was Joseph’s full brother and was initially kept in Canaan by Jacob rather than sent with his brothers to Egypt, reflecting Jacob’s concern for his safety.

During the famine, Joseph required Benjamin’s presence before providing further assistance to the family. Benjamin eventually traveled with his brothers to Egypt after an older brother pledged his safety. Joseph secretly placed his silver cup in Benjamin’s sack, causing him to be accused of theft; Benjamin’s sack was also found to contain the cup after Joseph had given him a portion five times larger than those of his brothers. When Joseph revealed his identity, he gave Benjamin three hundred pieces of silver and five changes of clothing.

In genealogical tradition, Benjamin is described as the father of Belah, Becher, Ashbel, Gera, Naaman, Ehi, Rosh, Muppim, Huppim, and Ard. Jacob’s prophetic blessing portrays Benjamin as a wolf that devours prey in the morning and divides the spoil at night.
